title: Discovering Paleolithic Korea
description: An extended journey through I.2.1 in the original KOREA chronology.

blocks.title: The evidence beneath our feet
paragraphs: Paleolithic Korea comes into view through traces left in the ground rather than through written testimony. Archaeologists work with layers of sediment, chipped stone, deposits from former river terraces, and the shifting locations of ancient waterways. What appears to be a simple implement may have passed through a long history of manufacturing, use, breakage, movement, and burial. Recovering it is only the beginning of reconstructing a human action. The interpreter must ask where the object was found, whether it remained in its original position, and what neighboring deposits may indicate about the setting.

This archaeological perspective makes the early history of the peninsula necessarily open-ended. Every excavation describes a sample of a far larger lost landscape, and different methods can lead to different chronological estimates. A visitor to a prehistoric site may see only a small cluster of stones behind museum glass. Behind those stones lies a difficult argument about the sequence of human arrival, the changing use of land, and the relationship between local evidence and developments elsewhere in Northeast Asia.

blocks.title: Stone as technology
paragraphs: A chipped stone tool is an answer to a material problem. Edges can cut, scrape, pierce, or help process other substances; their precise use cannot be assumed from shape alone. Toolmakers selected raw material, struck flakes from cores, and worked within constraints imposed by stone quality and availability. A valley rich in suitable cobbles offered different opportunities from a coastal landscape where people might need to transport preferred material from a distance.

The history of technology can therefore be approached as a history of decisions. A useful flake may be produced quickly and discarded immediately, whereas a carefully worked object may be transported and used repeatedly. Tool assemblages preserve fragments of these different strategies. They cannot automatically reveal how many people were present, what those people called themselves, or how social relations operated. Their importance lies in showing practical skill and adaptation across environments that themselves changed over thousands of years.

blocks.title: Cold, warm, and changing habitats
paragraphs: Prehistoric people did not inhabit one unchanging Korean peninsula. Climate, vegetation, coastlines, and animal distributions shifted over long periods. During colder intervals, landscapes and routes of movement could differ substantially from their later forms. River valleys might expose useful resources or form travel corridors, while high ground and seasonal conditions shaped what could be attempted. Such environmental patterns supply context, but they cannot be converted into a single rigid explanation for every archaeological site.

An accessible history should invite visitors to imagine the physical tasks of crossing a landscape without claiming to know the private thoughts of its inhabitants. Carrying tools, reading weather, finding fuel, and returning to a reliable source of water would all have had practical importance in many settings. Those observations describe general human challenges rather than documented scenes from one particular Korean camp. The distinction matters because the history is evocative precisely where the surviving record is incomplete.

blocks.title: What an excavation can and cannot tell us
paragraphs: An excavation operates by removing layers in a controlled sequence and documenting context before it disappears. Finds become more informative when associated with dates, sediment descriptions, other artifacts, and local geology. Modern interpretations also depend on laboratory techniques and comparison with material recovered elsewhere. The result is a cumulative conversation rather than a single dramatic discovery that settles every question about the first human occupation.

This subject is best explored through several parallel stories: the making of tools, the evolution of landscapes, the history of archaeological discovery, and the limits of assigning identity to people who left no written self-description. Those paths connect naturally to later Neolithic communities without implying that one culture simply turned into another overnight. The dividing lines in an encyclopedia help organize knowledge; the long human story itself did not arrive in neat chapters.

blocks.title: How a site becomes an archaeological argument
paragraphs: The first stage of archaeological work is not discovering a spectacular object. It is deciding what the surrounding deposit can still tell us. Before sediment is removed, its color, texture, boundaries, orientation, and relationship to geological events need to be recorded. A stone with unmistakable working scars has different evidential force when found in a sealed occupation horizon than when collected from a modern streambed. The latter may still be historically important, but it cannot anchor the same chronological claim. Careful site documentation makes possible a conversation across generations of scholars who cannot return an excavated layer to its original condition.

Archaeological interpretation is therefore both cumulative and destructive in a narrowly technical sense: excavation makes information available by removing the very context that preserved it. Photographs, drawings, geospatial measurements, and archived samples are not administrative extras. They are part of the evidence that later researchers will need when methods improve. A long-form history of Paleolithic Korea should show the reader how an apparently modest layer of gravel can support a major claim only after careful argument about formation, disturbance, and dating.

blocks.title: The handaxe as more than a museum symbol
paragraphs: A handaxe may attract attention because it looks purposefully shaped from several directions. Its surfaces can reveal deliberate removals, control of angles, and an anticipated form. Yet the category is broad, and not every shaped stone necessarily had the same function. Some may have served various cutting tasks; others could have been reduced or resharpened after long use. The problem is to connect form, manufacturing traces, wear, raw material, and context rather than permit the display case to answer every question.

The Jeongok-ri finds in the Hantan River region demonstrate this distinction. They became important in debates about East Asian stone industries because they challenged assumptions that bifacial handaxe technologies did not occur there. The National Museum of Korea recounts that scholarly turning point. But the historical lesson extends beyond one object: categorical lines drawn from incomplete distributions may be revised when excavations expand the sample. The appearance of a handaxe does not make its maker culturally identical to distant populations whose tools share a shape, and it cannot reveal a later national ancestry.

blocks.title: Reading the waste from manufacture
paragraphs: An excavator may recover many sharp fragments surrounding a stone core. To a nonspecialist the fragments can resemble accidental rubble. For a technological analyst they are the remains of a process, each with features that may help reconstruct how a maker struck the stone. Platforms, bulbs of percussion, scar directions, cortex, and broken edges can distinguish different reduction strategies. When fragments fit together physically, a sequence of removals may be reconstructed with unusual confidence.

The pieces that are missing matter too. A prepared blank might have been carried to another site. A durable tool could have been used elsewhere and returned only after repair. Some work may have relied on wood or fibers that vanished entirely. The archaeological assemblage is a residue of selected actions, not a complete toolkit. A history that counts finished implements while ignoring ordinary waste will misunderstand the scale and organization of stone working. The modest flake may tell a more precise story than the impressive handaxe because its place in a reduction sequence can be clearer.

blocks.title: The life of a raw material
paragraphs: Stone does not enter an archaeological site in a neutral form. Its availability and fracture properties shape technological choices. A river cobble offers a different starting point from stone extracted from a quarry-like exposure. A small piece of high-quality material may be carried carefully, while abundant coarse stone may be discarded after a short task. These choices concern labor, travel, anticipation, and the expected need for usable edges. Researchers can sometimes trace materials to geological sources, though visual resemblance alone is rarely enough for a secure provenance.

Transport creates a further interpretive difficulty. The nearest source on a modern map might not have been accessible in a particular prehistoric climate, and a raw material could change hands rather than be collected directly by its eventual user. A long-distance stone does not automatically establish a trading market or a permanent migration corridor. Its importance is that the archaeological account must expand from the excavation square into a network of possible movement, acquisition, maintenance, and discard. Even the apparent simplicity of a stone flake opens questions about economic choices.

blocks.title: Rivers and the selective preservation of time
paragraphs: Many early archaeological claims arise from terraces created by rivers over long periods. A terrace can preserve an ancient surface because sediment accumulated or a river changed its course. But water can also transport objects, mixing material from different locations and times. The archaeologist must distinguish a stable former land surface from redeposited artifacts and determine which sediment can legitimately be dated. A laboratory result may date the burying deposit, the underlying material, or an associated substance rather than the individual act of tool manufacture.

This technical caution should influence public historical writing. A map of earliest occupation dates can imply precision that the evidence does not warrant. Where dates are contested, readers deserve to know whether the disagreement concerns the artifact's human origin, the stratigraphy, the dating technique, or the interpretation of the resulting chronology. Uncertainty is not an embarrassment to be hidden at the end of the chapter. It is the substance of the earliest history, where better deposits and improved methods regularly alter the questions that can be asked.
blocks.label: Batch P · original evidence-sensitive continuation

blocks.title: People missing from stone-centered histories
paragraphs: Paleolithic archaeology excels at recording durable stone but struggles to recover daily labor involving perishable materials. Woodworking, food gathering, caring for children, carrying water, preparing hides, or maintaining a place to sleep may have involved fewer objects likely to survive. An archive dominated by tools therefore risks creating a past dominated by toolmakers. Human communities also include differences in age, bodily ability, expertise, and circumstance that cannot easily be separated in a scatter of broken rock.

Recognition of this problem does not justify inventing particular families or assigning rigid gendered tasks to remote populations. Instead, historians can ask which indispensable forms of work are likely to be invisible, which could leave indirect traces, and what kinds of evidence would strengthen a claim. This approach makes the narrative fuller without pretending that empathy can substitute for archaeology. It also prevents the most technically elaborate artifacts from monopolizing the account of human achievement.

blocks.title: The boundaries of a prehistoric map
paragraphs: The landscape now called the Korean peninsula was part of Northeast Asia before the existence of the states and names that dominate later history. Archaeological distributions should therefore be compared across present borders while remaining alert to changes in sea level, rivers, and ecological corridors. Similar stone industries in neighboring regions can raise hypotheses about contact or shared methods, but they do not automatically demonstrate a single people. Technological resemblance must be interpreted with chronology, raw material, and site formation in view.

Prehistory has often been recruited into arguments about national origins because people naturally want long histories of belonging. The discipline can acknowledge that interest while refusing to project later political categories backward. The earliest inhabitants left no inscriptions identifying themselves as Koreans; even biological continuity cannot be inferred simply from sequential occupation of a territory. The historical achievement is to reconstruct human activity on its own evidential terms, not force archaeological findings to certify a modern identity.

blocks.title: Why discoveries change the questions
paragraphs: A new excavation may produce an unfamiliar tool form, a better-preserved layer, or material suitable for dating. Such discoveries can refine a regional sequence, but rarely remove every uncertainty. Sometimes they complicate an apparently simple progression by revealing technological coexistence or different local trajectories. Reexamining an old collection with new analytical techniques may be equally consequential. The history of Paleolithic research is consequently a history of changing methods as well as a history of early human occupation.

This makes a broad encyclopedia different from a timeline of celebrated discoveries. Each site matters because it contributes to an argument about movement, work, environment, or chronology, and the same site may support different questions with different degrees of certainty. An effective reader should be able to follow those arguments without having to accept the most dramatic claim attached to a find. Archaeology is at its strongest when the surviving object and the limits of its interpretation remain visible together.
